correctness.rationale: Primitive Fourier frequency collisions require count-vector differences to be multiples of \((-(B-A),B,-A)\), so no moment \(r<B\) has a phase term and exactly one pair contributes at \(r=B\). Exact coefficient bookkeeping yields the stated normalized cosine amplitude. Strict weighted-product concavity yields unique squared-amplitude ratios \((B-A):B:A\) and the exact optimal radius. The quadrature identity and Euclidean argument differential give sharp inverse conditioning and deterministic angular bound. The universal bound follows from binomial probability, balanced asymptotics from Stirling. A standalone checker reproduced 614 finite collision instances plus sharp rational radii. The all-pairs proof is symbolic; finite checking is not treated as an infinite proof.

value.rationale: The theorem answers the exact motivated inverse-design question of how to allocate fixed Fourier coefficient power to maximize the earliest detectable relative-phase observable and minimize two-probe inverse amplification. It gives a unique, non-equal optimal power ratio and a universal exponential loss of optimal sensitivity as the primitive gap grows, with a matching-rate balanced family. That phase-observability obstruction is a substantive structural fact, not a rounding/checking exercise, albeit limited to three lines and known amplitudes.
